scenes.narration: A Greek historian was told how the Great Pyramid was built. A hundred thousand men, he wrote, working in gangs of three months each. Was he right?

data.text: They worked in gangs of a hundred thousand men, each gang for three months.

scenes.narration: Let's count the builders ourselves, using what they left behind. Their town, their tombs, and the logbook of one of their inspectors. From the Giza plateau to a desert harbour on the Red Sea.
The ancient numbers only grew. Herodotus gave a hundred thousand. Diodorus gave three hundred sixty thousand. But Herodotus wrote, they said. Diodorus wrote, as they say. Neither man counted anyone.

And neither man was there. Herodotus probably reached Egypt sometime after four hundred fifty four BC. The pyramid was already more than two thousand years old. He stood about as far from Khufu as we stand from Julius Caesar.

data.label: The pyramid when Herodotus saw it: c. 2600 BC vs after 454 BC

scenes.narration: Read literally, Herodotus says even more. A new gang of a hundred thousand every three months means four gangs a year. That is four hundred thousand men, every single year.

data.label: Four gangs of 100,000, three months each

scenes.narration: Read him closely, and the word slaves never appears. He says the king compelled Egyptians to work. Ten years went on the road, and twenty on the pyramid itself.

data.title: What Herodotus actually wrote
items: The king “compelled all the Egyptians to work”
Gangs of 100,000 men, three months each
Ten years for the road, twenty for the pyramid

scenes.narration: Yet the slave story keeps being repeated. In two thousand ten, a news agency report said Herodotus described the builders as slaves. As we just read, he did not. The same report says Egyptologists blame Hollywood for spreading the myth.

data.text: The ancient Greek historian Herodotus once described the pyramid builders as slaves

scenes.narration: Now the size of the job. The pyramid holds an estimated two point three million blocks. Together they weigh about six million tonnes, and it stood about one hundred forty seven metres tall.

data.label: About 6,000,000 tonnes of stone in all

scenes.narration: Not all that stone was local. Most blocks were quarried right on the Giza plateau. The fine white casing came from Tura, across the river. And granite for the king's chamber came from Aswan, far to the south.
Aswan lies about six hundred eighty kilometres south of Giza, in a straight line. Some of its granite blocks weighed up to eighty tonnes. Even so, they ended up at the heart of the pyramid.
Spread over Herodotus's twenty years, that is about three hundred fifteen blocks every day. In daylight, one block every two or three minutes. So how many hands does that take?

data.label: 2.3 million blocks over 20 years, every day of the year

scenes.narration: That pace sounds impossible, and some people use it to argue the pyramid was not built by hand. Lehner's answer is simple. The stones did not go in one after another. Many teams worked at once.

data.text: But the stones didn't go in one after another, you see.

scenes.narration: Lehner tested it. In a NOVA experiment, twelve men pulled a one and a half ton block across a slick surface with ease. Moving stone did not need armies. It needed well drilled teams.

data.label: NOVA pulling experiment, described by Mark Lehner

scenes.narration: From there he worked out the rest. About twelve hundred men in the quarry, and two thousand hauling. Add the stone setters, and the total for twenty years of work is five thousand men or fewer.

data.title: Lehner's count for a twenty-year build

scenes.narration: The modern answer starts in the sand. In nineteen eighty eight, archaeologists began digging a lost town south of the Sphinx. In nineteen ninety, a tourist's horse stumbled on the builders' tombs. Then came a logbook.

events.label: A tourist's horse stumbles on the builders' tombs

scenes.narration: The town covered more than seven hectares. The crown built it, with bakeries, workshops and royal grain silos. It looks less like a slave camp than a supply base.

data.label: The workers' town, 400 m south of the Sphinx

scenes.narration: At its centre stood a royal administrative building with ten massive grain silos. Grain came in, and bread and beer went out to the workforce. In Arabic, the site is called the Wall of the Crow.

The tombs point the same way. Zahi Hawass, then Egypt's archaeology chief, said slaves would never have been buried so honorably. Some tombs even held jars that once contained beer and bread, provisions for the afterlife.

data.text: No way would they have been buried so honorably if they were slaves.
data.source: Egypt's archaeology chief, to the Associated Press, 2010

scenes.narration: The skeletons also show medical care. Twelve workers had injured hands supported with wood. One man's leg was crushed by a stone and cut off. He lived fourteen more years. The workers he studied died between thirty and thirty five.

data.label: after a crushed leg was amputated (Hawass, NOVA)

scenes.narration: But not slaves is not the same as free. The archaeologist Mark Lehner asks whether they were conscripts. Hawass describes crews rotating in, three months at a time.

data.caption: Not slaves is not the same as free

scenes.narration: The builders also left their own names. Gangs painted them on blocks, even in hidden chambers above the king's burial chamber. One gang was the Friends of Khufu. Another called itself the Drunkards of Menkaure.

data.text: the Friends of Khufu gang, the Drunks of Menkaura gang

scenes.narration: Lehner reads the graffiti like an organisation chart. Each gang had two crews. Each crew had five phyles, from the Greek word for tribe. Each phyle had divisions, with names meaning endurance, perfection and strong.
That logbook belonged to an inspector named Merer. He ran a crew of about forty men, late in King Khufu's reign. His logbook records the work day by day.

data.label: Tallet's estimate, from the logbook of Khufu's year 26–27

scenes.narration: Merer's journal was found in two thousand thirteen, at an ancient harbour on the Red Sea coast. That is about a hundred nineteen kilometres south of Suez. It is the oldest surviving papyrus document, more than four and a half thousand years old.
They shipped fine limestone by boat from the quarries at Tura to the pyramid. One boat may have carried about thirty blocks. The short round trip took about two days.
Merer's trips ran from July to November. That was the flood season, when the Nile rose by six or seven metres. High water was the only practical time for big cargo boats.

Crews also combined for big jobs. For ten days, Merer's men worked on a dam. On one day they joined about fifteen other phyles, perhaps six hundred more men. Their supervisor was most likely Ankh-haf, overseer of all the king's works.

data.label: Merer's phyle plus some 15 others (Tallet, via Lehner)

scenes.narration: Back at the town, long galleries look like barracks. A crew of about forty, like Merer's, would just fit inside one. The workforce came in units we can count.

Modern estimates disagree, but look at their size. Lehner counts about five thousand core builders. Hawass has said twenty thousand, and thirty six thousand. A contractor's ten year schedule peaks at forty thousand.

data.title: Modern estimates, from core crew to peak

scenes.narration: Hawass sees the pyramid as a national project. Households, he says, sent food to feed the workmen, and everyone took part. It is a generous reading of the evidence, but it fits the bakeries and the silos.

data.text: the households will send food to feed the workmen

scenes.narration: Even the highest modern estimate is well under Herodotus's hundred thousand. His figure is two and a half times bigger, and Diodorus's is nine times. They measured different things, but they were the wrong size.

left.label: Herodotus
left.note: Hearsay, written down by a Greek historian.

scenes.narration: Here is what we still don't know. How many men cut stone far away, at Aswan and Tura. How many blocks there really are. Even Hawass has given figures from ten thousand to thirty six thousand.

data.title: What we still don't know
items: How many cut stone far away, at Aswan and Tura
How many blocks there really are
Why one expert's figures run from 10,000 to 36,000

scenes.narration: So, a hundred thousand men in gangs of three months? No. Thousands, tens of thousands at the peak, and every one of them had to eat. Hawass estimated twenty one cattle and twenty three sheep a day.
Over a year, that is more than seven thousand six hundred cattle. Moving the stone was hard. Feeding the people who moved it may have been the bigger job.
The Great Pyramid was not built by a vast slave army. It was built by organised crews, housed, fed and buried with honour. Next, why half of Rome survived nearly a thousand years longer.

data.title: Housed, fed and buried with honour
